nameStory: Common boneset gets its unusual name from its historical use in treating dengue fever, which was also called "break-bone fever" because of the intense bone and joint pain it caused. Native Americans introduced this medicinal plant to European colonists, who discovered it could "set" or heal those terrible bone-aching fevers by causing heavy sweating. The plant was so valued as a fever-breaker that it earned nicknames like "feverwort" and "sweating-plant."
description: Common boneset is a sturdy perennial wildflower that grows 2-4 feet tall in wet meadows and swamps throughout New England. Its most distinctive feature is how the narrow, lance-shaped leaves appear to be pierced right through by the hairy stem, creating a unique "perfoliate" look. In late summer, the plant tops itself with clusters of small, fuzzy white flowers that look like tiny cotton balls, attracting butterflies and other pollinators to wetland areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The stem appears to pierce directly through the middle of each wrinkled, lance-shaped leaf - imagine threading a straw through paper. Leaves are rough-textured with prominent veins and feel somewhat sandpapery when rubbed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, flat-topped clusters of small white flowers that look like miniature shaving cream puffs. Each tiny flower head contains only disc flowers (no petals), giving the whole cluster a fuzzy, cotton-ball appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stands 2-4 feet tall with a sturdy, unbranched stem that's noticeably hairy and often has a grayish appearance. The plant grows in clumps and has a robust, upright posture even in wet soils.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found with "wet feet" - look for it in swamps, wet meadows, ditches, and streambanks where the soil stays consistently moist. Rarely found in dry upland areas.

habitat: Common boneset thrives in New England's wetlands, from sea level to moderate elevations. Look for it in swamps, wet meadows, marshes, roadside ditches, and along stream banks where the soil stays consistently moist or even seasonally flooded. It often grows alongside other moisture-loving plants like joe-pye weed, swamp milkweed, and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fuzzy shoots with the characteristic perfoliate leaves already visible, making identification possible even when young.
seasonality.summer: Reaches full height by midsummer with mature perfoliate leaves clearly displayed. Flower buds begin forming in late July.
seasonality.fall: Blooms from August through September with distinctive white, fuzzy flower clusters. Seeds develop into fluffy, dandelion-like heads that disperse in autumn winds.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving dried stems that may persist into early winter before breaking down completely.

funFact: Boneset was so trusted as a fever remedy that it was officially listed in the U.S. Pharmacopoeia (the official drug reference book) from 1820 to 1916, making it one of the few Native American medicines to achieve formal medical recognition in early America.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other white-flowered wetland plants, but the perfoliate leaves (stem piercing through leaf) are a dead giveaway - no other common wetland plant in New England has this feature. Remember: "boneset leaves look like they've been threaded like a bead on a string."
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this plant with comfrey, which is also sometimes called "boneset" in herbal circles but is a completely different European plant with different leaves and blue or purple flowers. True boneset is purely a North American native with white flowers and perfoliate leaves.
compareHints: Among its Eupatorium relatives, common boneset is the only one with perfoliate leaves where the stem pierces through the leaf base. Joe-pye weeds (also Eupatorium) have whorled leaves and pink-purple flowers, while other bonesets like upland boneset have separate, paired leaves that don't clasp the stem. The white, flat-topped flower clusters also distinguish it from the dome-shaped pink clusters of joe-pye weeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the bonesets, hyssopleaf thoroughwort stands out immediately for its extremely narrow leaves—while common boneset has broad, wrinkled leaves that clasp the stem, and rough boneset has lance-shaped leaves, this species looks almost grass-like.

Among the boneset family, rough boneset stands out for its notably hairy, rough-textured leaves and stems, while common boneset has distinctive leaves that appear "perforated" by the stem passing through them.
Among the boneset family, late boneset stands out for its very late bloom time and alternate leaf arrangement.

Among the many boneset species, upland boneset is distinguished by its narrow, stalkless leaves that don't wrap around the stem like common boneset, and its preference for dry habitats unlike most other bonesets.
Unlike common boneset which has leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, New England boneset has clearly separate opposite leaves.
Among the boneset family, tall boneset stands out with its alternate leaf arrangement (most other bonesets have opposite leaves) and its particularly dense, flat-topped flower clusters.
Among its boneset relatives, roundleaf thoroughwort is the wetland specialist with the roundest, softest leaves.
Among its boneset relatives in New England, dogfennel is unmistakable due to its incredibly fine, thread-like leaves - all other Eupatorium species have broad, simple leaves.
Hemp agrimony stands out immediately from all native New England Eupatorium species because of its deeply divided, palm-shaped leaves – every other boneset in our region has simple, undivided leaves.
Unlike common boneset which has distinctive perfoliate leaves that appear to be pierced by the stem, Torrey's eupatorium has narrow, separate leaves.
Unlike common boneset with its perforated leaves that wrap around the stem, veined thoroughwort has clearly separate opposite leaves.
